newsitem.title: INDIA: India minister says oil bill backlog critical - PTI.
newsitem.headline: India minister says oil bill backlog critical - PTI.

text.p: India's Petroleum Minister Janeshwar Mishra warned on Thursday that a $4.9 billion backlog of payments due to oil companies had become critical and imported crude supplies could be hit soon, Press Trust of India said.
Indian oil companies are owed around 175 billion rupees by the government for selling below market prices to support the country's subsidy regime.
The oil pool account deficit has grown by around 20 billion rupees since the beginning of the 1997/98 financial year on April 1, when the deficit stood at 155 billion rupees.

Mishra said in an interview with the news agency Indian Oil Corp, the country's only importing agency, faced difficulties importing as it had already borrowed 140 billion rupees ($3.9 billion) and was owed 90 billion from the oil pool account.
"Under the present circumstances, imports may dry up," he warned.
The United Front steering committee, which agrees policy for the coalition government, has met twice unsuccessfully to figure how to whittle down the oil pool deficit.

A third meeting has been deferred several times, the latest postponement coming on July 8 and no new date has been set although Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has said the issue should be settled this month.
India's oil import bills rose 41 per cent to nearly $9.0 billion 1996-97 and IOC exhausted as much as $2.2 billion of its $2.9 billion dollar external commercial borrowing limit.

"We are working on various ways as to how the oil pool deficit of 155 billion rupees (till March 31, 1997) is to be met and are seeking to devise measures so that new loans are not created," Mishra said.
Mishra, who was appointed a month ago, appeared to dampen hopes of one potential source of money to pull the oil pool out of the red.

He said the Finance Ministry was unlikely to make good 43 billion rupees swiped from for the oil pool by a previous government when the oil account was in surplus, but added that he would raise objections with the Finance Ministry.
Some analysts had speculated that the government could offer to issue bonds to replace the money which oil companbies could then hold or sell on the secondary market.
"Do you really think it is practical to expect the money back after ten years when the Finance Ministry could always say it had spent the money on development, roads and hospitals," Mishra said.
He said domestic production was also under pressure as output from the Bombay High field came under strain and separatist violence in the north-east jeopardised production from Assam.
"We will have to think in terms of going deeper into the sea for exploration for which the country will necessarily have to develop or acquire technology," Mishra said.

The government is also reportedly working on major tax incentives, including higher depreciation and corporate tax concessions to attract fresh foreign and domestic investment in the petroleum sector, besides formulating a new "oil code".
